title: egress-segmentation-and-stub-dns-migration-notes
body:
Purpose:

Quick, pragmatic design + migration plan for: (1) segmenting customer egress in private deployments so each tenant has stable outbound IPs and observable rules, and (2) migrating local stub resolver deployment from per-node dnsmasq to a resilient conditional-forwarding fabric (supports split-horizon with customer resolvers). Goal is a low-risk upgrade path that works both for VPC-hosted Private control plane and on-prem appliance installs.

Scope and constraints:

- Applicable to Private deployments (VPC and on-prem) where customers require predictable egress IPs, auditability, and optional tenant-level firewalling.
- Must not require changes to customer application code.
- Minimize downtime; target rolling upgrade with per-tenant canaries.
- Support mixed kube versions (1.24 - 1.27) and both Calico and Cilium network policies.
- Assume customers may have their own resolver appliances; solution must support conditional forwarding and respecting customer stub TTLs.

Assumptions:

- We control an egress gateway set (baremetal or cloud instances) per region.
- We can allocate NAT pools or announce egress prefixes via customer BGP in on-prem installs.
- K8s clusters have an egress annotation surface or can be fronted by a service mesh sidecar (if requested).

High-level design:

1) Egress segmentation
- Provision one or more egress gateways per site/region (egress-appliance-0..N).
- Map tenant -> egress-group. An egress-group is a logical token that binds: outbound CIDR/NAT pool + firewall policy + optional external-BGP advertisement.
- Requests from tenant workloads are routed (via iptables/iptables-nft rules or BPF redirect) to the assigned egress gateway. SNAT is applied using the egress-group NAT pool so customer sees fixed outbound IP(s).
- Observability: each gateway exports per-tenant counters (bytes, flows, TCP/UDP breakdown) to Prometheus and logs connection metadata to structured logs (for SOC/audit).

2) Stub DNS migration (per-node dnsmasq -> forwarding fabric)
- Replace per-node dnsmasq with a lightweight cluster-local resolver layer: a HA set of stub-resolvers (dns-proxy pods or small HA appliances) that run on control plane or dedicated nodes.
- Conditional forwarding rules: for customer split-horizon zones (e.g., corp.example.com), forward to customer-provided resolvers over TLS (stubby/DoT) or mTLS-protected TCP. Fall back to upstream public resolvers if customer resolvers fail and policy allows.
- Cache TTLs must be honored; expose a config for aggressive TTL overrides for private zones only if requested.

Terraform module notes (practical API and implementation caveats)

- Proposed modules: module "priv_egress_gateway" and module "priv_dns_forwarder"

module priv_egress_gateway (inputs):
- tenants: map(string -> object)  # key: tenant_id, value: {egress_group = string, allowed_ports = list, policy_profile = string}
- egress_groups: map(string -> object)  # e.g. nat_pool_cidrs, bgp_announce, gateway_count
- gateway_instance_type: string
- network_interface_ids: list(string)
- tenant_annotation_prefix: string (default: "x-rw-tenant")
- cloud_mode: string ("gcp"|"aws"|"onprem")

outputs:
- gateway_ips: map(string)  # egress_group -> list of IPs
- tenant_routes: list(string)  # iptables/ip route objects for agent application

Implementation notes / gotchas:
- Use provider-agnostic TF constructs for resource tagging; avoid cloud-provider-specific features for onprem module variant.
- NAT pool assignment must be idempotent: keep a terraform state map {egress_group -> allocated_cidr}. Use a small allocator helper (external data source script) to avoid collisions.
- For on-prem, we prefer programmatic BGP announcement via Bird/FRR on the gateway hosts; document required customer L2/L3 handoff VLANs.
- Plan for ephemeral egress (short-lived workload IPs) — ensure SNAT mapping cache expiry is long enough so connection tracking doesn't break long-lived flows.

module priv_dns_forwarder (inputs):
- forward_zones: map(string -> list(string)) # zone -> list of upstream IPs or DoT endpoints
- tls_profiles: map(string -> object) # optional: {client_cert, ca_cert, sni}
- mode: string ("k8s-pod"|"node-daemonset"|"appliance")
- retention_seconds: number  # cache retention override

outputs:
- forwarder_ips: list(string)
- applied_forward_rules: list(string)

Implementation notes:
- Use CoreDNS with plugin configuration when running as pods; CoreDNS supports conditional forwarding and TLS via the forward plugin (with tls and force_tcp options).
- When running as an appliance, use unbound/dnsdist for more advanced TLS/mTLS forwarding and higher QPS.
- Test resolvers with "dig +short @forwarder zone SOA" and systemd-resolve check.

Migration / Upgrade plan (phased)

Phase 0 - Preparation (preflight):
- Inventory current clusters: per-cluster existing egress IP behavior, per-node dns resolver config, customer split-horizon zones and resolvers. (script: scripts/inventory-egress.sh)
- Allocate egress_group NAT pools in TF staging state (dry-run).
- Run compatibility tests for BPF redirect vs iptables on target kernel versions.

Phase 1 - Deploy egress gateways (shadow mode):
- Provision gateways and configure to accept mirrored traffic.
- Start mirroring (tcpdump/IP mirror) from a small set of tenant namespaces to the gateway to validate policy mapping, but do not SNAT yet. Collect metrics for 48-72 hours.

Phase 2 - DNS forwarder pilot:
- Deploy CoreDNS forwarder in cluster-pool mode; route a handful of pods to use it via k8s dnsPolicy + stubdomains.
- Validate conditional-forwarding reachability and failover behavior with chaos tests (bring customer resolver down).

Phase 3 - Controlled SNAT rollout (canary tenants):
- For 1–2 low-risk tenants, add iptables rules or iproute2 rules to redirect their outbound through gateway and apply SNAT using their egress_group pool.
- Monitor: external IP validation (curl checkip), TCP/UDP health, connection tracking metrics, application-level smoke tests.

Phase 4 - Full tenant migration:
- Batch migrate remaining tenants in waves. For each wave: apply TF change (update mapping), run post-hooks (check routes, NAT mapping), promote metrics to dashboards and run audit logs export to S3.

Rollback strategy:

- DNS forwarder regress: repoint node-level resolv.conf to original dnsmasq, scale down forwarder.
- SNAT rollback per-tenant: remove redirect rule and restore original iptables chain. Maintain an automated script that re-applies pre-upgrade iptables state from backup.
- If BGP announcement causes route leaks, withdraw announcement immediately and escalate to network on-call.

Testing checklists (pre-merge and post-deploy):

Pre-merge:
- TF plan is deterministic across runs. No random allocator in tests.
- Unit tests for terraform modules (terratest) covering allocator edge cases.

Post-deploy:
- For each tenant: verify 3x outbound IPs (dig to checkip service), 5-minute slow start checks for long-lived TCP connections, validate DNS resolution for split-horizon zones from within pod, and verify logs contain tenant tag.
- Run adverse condition tests: drop packets to upstream resolvers (simulate flapping), CPU stress on gateway to verify graceful degradation.

Observability and SLOs:

- SLO targets for migration: <1% DNS query failure increase, <2% latency regression for resolved hostnames, and fewer than 10 failed customer connectivity incidents during migration window per region.
- Expose per-tenant egress metrics in "private-deployments/egress" Prometheus job. Add Kibana dashboards for DNS forwarder latency and query rates.

Security and compliance notes:

- Customer data in DNS queries may be sensitive; forwarder must have logging toggle per-customer. Default: obfuscate query names in logs; provide opt-in cleartext logging for customers who request it.
- mTLS for forwarders when configured; store certs in customer's KMS or provide short-lived client certs via control plane CA.

Open questions / decisions needed:

- Per-tenant IP count: what is default pool size (1 vs 3)? Operational trade-offs documented but we need policy decision.
- Do we allow fallback to public resolvers for split-horizon zones when customer resolvers fail? (Default: no, but configurable.)
- Onprem BGP: do we require customer to allocate a /29 per tenant for full visibility, or can we map multiple tenants to a single /28 and track via logs?

Action items (owners):

- Rohit: build terratest harness for egress allocator (due 2025-10-02).
- Maya: prototype CoreDNS config with DoT and conditional forwarder for two test zones (due 2025-10-07).
- Diego: create gateway provisioning playbook for on-prem installs (BGP bird config, VLAN checklist) (due 2025-10-09).
- Ava: coordinate canary tenant list and communication plan with solutions engineering, and draft rollback runbook (due 2025-10-05).

Notes to self / rough sketches:

- Keep DNS forwarder config in git per-customer - avoid baking certs into TF state. Use secrets manager references.
- Consider a lightweight eBPF redirect for lower-latency forwarding on newer kernels; fallback to iptables for older hosts.

Appendix: quick CoreDNS forward plugin example (for reference)

- Corefile snippet:
  example.com:53 {
    forward . tls://10.1.2.3:853 {
      tls_servername example-cust-resolver
      policy sequential
    }
    cache 30
  }

- iptables redirect example (one-liner prototype):
  iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -m owner --uid-owner tenant_uid -j DNAT --to-destination 10.20.30.5

End of notes.
